name: Sanganeri hand block printing
summary: Sanganeri hand block printing is a hand block-printed textile tradition of Sanganer town, about 16 km from Jaipur, registered as a Geographical Indication (application no. 147) by the Calico Printers Co-operative Society. It is known for fine, repetitive floral butis and butas on a white ground, printed by Chhipa printers with blocks carved by Kharadi block-makers, traditionally using a harda (myrobalan) pre-treatment, iron (syahi) and alum (begar) mordants dyed in alizarin/madder, sun-bleaching, dabu mud-resist and indigo. Since the 1960s the craft has faced competition from screen printing and a large shift to synthetic dyes, and the cluster is associated with documented water pollution.

concepts.title: Migration of printers and Jaipur royal patronage
concepts.summary: Oral tradition, said to be confirmed by archival sources, holds that Sawai Jai Singh invited craftsmen to Jaipur, including printers from Gujarat; Malwa craftsmen are conjectured too.
concepts.body_md:
Oral tradition, said to be confirmed by archival sources, holds that Sawai Jai Singh invited craftsmen to Jaipur, including printers from Gujarat; Malwa craftsmen are conjectured too. [S1, S10]

The craft is widely believed to have arisen from mid-17th-century Mughal and Maratha campaigns in Gujarat that forced printers from Kathiawar to migrate to Rajasthan, including Sanganer. [S9]

Gaatha says mid-17th-century upheavals may have forced Gujarati printers to flee to Sanganer in the Dhundhar region. [S8]

The V&A describes Sanganer as a centre for high-quality block-printed cotton, established to serve the Jaipur court and encouraged by Jaipur royal patronage. [S5, S6]

concepts.title: Archival evidence from the 18th and 19th centuries
concepts.summary: East India Company records of the 16th and 17th centuries do not name Sanganer; dastur-al-amal reports of 1703 and rangkhana records of 1727 describe taxes on printed fabrics.
concepts.body_md:
East India Company records of the 16th and 17th centuries do not name Sanganer; dastur-al-amal reports of 1703 and rangkhana records of 1727 describe taxes on printed fabrics. [S1]

A head-dress in the City Palace collection carries an octroi seal dated V.S. 1856 (A.D. 1799), and dupattas printed at Sanganer carry dated octroi stamps such as 1853 and 1906. [S1]

State archival records are available from 1727 onward, and no record of a Sanganer printing unit is traced before the 18th century. [S10]

Sir George Watt (Indian Art at Delhi, 1902-03) called Sanganer the metropolis of the calico-printing craft of India for art conceptions and technique. [S1, S10]

concepts.title: Screen printing, synthetic dyes and revival (1960s onward)
concepts.summary: Screen printing entered Sanganer around 1960 through Khatri migrants from Mirpur and Sind, and many printing families adopted mill cloth, synthetic dyes and screens.
concepts.body_md:
Screen printing entered Sanganer around 1960 through Khatri migrants from Mirpur and Sind, and many printing families adopted mill cloth, synthetic dyes and screens. [S10]

Screen printing emerged in Sanganer in the 1960s as a cheaper, faster method using synthetic dyes, and some block printers also adopted synthetic dyes. [S12]

Over the preceding decades a large number of screen-printing units arose, and screen-printed 'Sanganeri' textiles were being sold across India. [S1]

The craft was revived in the 1970s with patrons including Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and Anokhi; floods in 1981 set the industry back, and Sanganer joined a UNIDO cluster programme in 1997. [S10]

Gaatha says chemical dyes were introduced in the 1980s and widened the range of colours. [S8]

concepts.title: Dyeing effluent, the Amanishah Nallah and groundwater

Eleven groundwater samples from Sanganer were polluted by percolation of this wastewater; iron was found in almost all sources. [S11]
